system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2154-03-01 10:30:00 to 2154-03-08 16:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, and hypertension was admitted for nausea, vomiting, fever, and coffee-ground emesis. He was found to have influenza, which explained his fevers and gastrointestinal symptoms. An upper GI bleed was suspected due to the emesis, but endoscopy was deferred due to a vagal episode causing hypotension. His hemoglobin dropped but stabilized without transfusion. A new diagnosis of systolic heart failure was made after an echocardiogram showed reduced ejection fraction, prompting cardiology consultation and medication adjustments. Possible Chagas cardiomyopathy was identified via serology, with recommendations sent to primary care. Pleural effusions and wheezing were managed with diuresis and albuterol. He completed a dialysis session during admission for hyperkalemia and was discharged stable on day four with follow-up plans for cardiology and pulmonary function testing.
problems: Diabetes with renal manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

procedures.long_title: Extracorporeal circulation auxiliary to open heart surgery

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , part of the cardiothoracic team. You're here today for your scheduled coronary artery bypass surgery because of severe blockages in three of your heart arteries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been having more chest pain lately, especially when I walk. Is this surgery going to help with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’re doing a quadruple bypass—four grafts—to restore blood flow to your heart muscle. That should significantly reduce or even eliminate your chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And because of my diabetes and dialysis, is this riskier for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It does carry higher risk, yes, but your team has reviewed everything. Your dialysis access is stable, and we’ll manage your blood sugar closely. The benefits outweigh the risks given your symptoms and heart function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. When will it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're going to the operating room in about an hour. We’ll put you to sleep, and the surgery will take several hours. Your family can wait in the surgical waiting area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___ , you're back in the ICU. The surgery went well—you had a CABG x4 with the internal mammary and vein grafts successfully placed. You're still on the breathing machine for now, but we’ll wean you off soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mmm… okay… glad it went okay…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You were extubated this morning—off the ventilator—and doing well. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My throat’s a little sore, and my chest hurts, but I can breathe fine. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep managing your pain and get you up in a chair today. You’ll also have dialysis later—we scheduled it for noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m on dialysis three times a week usually—will we keep that schedule?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your regular dialysis schedule while you're here. Your kidney function is stable, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis went smoothly. But we noticed your blood sugar spiked earlier—it hit 320. We’ve consulted endocrinology to help manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been hard to control lately. I’m on insulin, but it’s tricky with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The endocrinology team will adjust your insulin—likely switching to a basal-bolus regimen. We may move you back to the ICU tonight for closer monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to ICU? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s precautionary. High sugars after heart surgery can increase infection risk, so we want to be very careful. You’re not unstable, but we’ll watch you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood sugar is improving. We’re keeping you on the new insulin plan: glargine in the morning and humalog before meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I go back to the regular floor soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. Your chest tubes are draining less, so we’ll remove them soon. We’ll also check a chest X-ray after removal to make sure there’s no air leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We removed your chest tubes this morning. The X-ray shows no pneumothorax—great news. You’re now back on the regular floor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My chest feels a little better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also gave you a beta-blocker this morning to help your heart work more efficiently, but you became bradycardic—your heart rate dropped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did I pass out? I felt dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you stayed alert, and your blood pressure was okay. We stopped the beta-blocker and will restart it slowly later. Your temporary pacing wires are now off since your rhythm stabilized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We transfused one unit of packed red cells today. Your hemoglobin was low at 9.2, likely from the surgery and chronic kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’ve been feeling tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. The transfusion should help with that. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed some drainage from the lower part of your chest incision—serosanguinous, not pus. Your white count is normal, and you’re not running a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely, but we’re starting you on cephalexin as a precaution. We also did a chest X-ray, which shows a moderate fluid collection on the left side—pleural effusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that go away on its own?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s common after heart surgery. You’re not short of breath, and your oxygen levels are good, so we’ll just monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound is looking better, and the drainage has decreased. You’re finishing day two of antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge on day seven—this Sunday. Physical therapy will evaluate you tomorrow to make sure you’re safe to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: PT cleared you for discharge. You can walk independently and manage stairs. We’ll go over your discharge instructions today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue aspirin, a new statin—pravastatin—and omeprazole for your reflux. We’re also continuing your insulin: glargine and humalog on a sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the cephalexin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, finish the full five-day course. Also, captopril for blood pressure and heart protection, and fenofibrate for your triglycerides.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help at home, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll have home health services. No driving for a month, no lifting more than 10 pounds for 10 weeks, and no creams on the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your regular schedule. Call if you gain more than two pounds in a day or five in a week—could be fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my incision looks red or drains more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us immediately. Also report any fever over 101. We want to catch any infection early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your final chest X-ray shows the effusion is stable. You’re cleared for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your prescriptions to your pharmacy. You’ll follow up with cardiology, your primary doctor, and nephrology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart—will it keep getting stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with the bypass grafts, blood flow is restored. Continue your meds, control your sugars, and attend cardiac rehab when cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Take care, and call with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just a little sore, but I’m feeling okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep up the deep breathing exercises and walking. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is here. They’ll take you home safely with your care instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doctor. I’ll follow everything you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up. Take it easy and heal well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your MRSA screen came back negative, so no infection risk there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All part of being thorough. You’re in good shape for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand not to drive while on pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I won’t drive until I’m off the hydromorphone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And keep monitoring your weight and incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve written it all down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your oxygen levels are 97% on room air. You’re good to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you in the clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick call to confirm—your prescriptions are ready at the pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll pick them up on the way home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your echocardiogram showed biventricular cardiomyopathy, so keep following with cardiology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I know my heart’s been weak for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bypass should help. Keep managing your diabetes and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I really appreciate your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care and heal well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll be in touch if anything comes up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type I diabetes, and severe coronary artery disease underwent a quadruple coronary artery bypass graft (CABG x4) for revascularization. Postoperatively, he remained intubated overnight and was extubated on postoperative day one. He experienced transient hyperglycemia requiring ICU readmission and insulin regimen adjustment with endocrinology consultation. A serosanguinous sternal wound drainage prompted a course of cephalexin, and a moderate left pleural effusion was noted but remained asymptomatic. He received hemodialysis throughout the admission and a single unit of packed red cells for anemia. He was successfully weaned from inotropic support, transferred to the floor, and cleared for discharge home on postoperative day seven with home health services. Discharge instructions emphasized wound care, activity restrictions, and close monitoring for signs of infection or fluid overload.
